claims.text: Controlled high-fluence helium irradiation of refractory HEAs will create a fine, dense dispersion of sub-10 nm helium bubbles.
Helium bubbles created by irradiation act as dislocation-pinning centers.
Irradiation-induced helium bubbles increase yield strength.
The helium-irradiation treatment preserves phase stability under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The helium-irradiation treatment preserves chemical homogeneity and prevents macroscopic elemental segregation.
Hf1Ta-like refractory HEAs have a single-phase, near-equiatomic initial structure with established baseline mechanical properties.
Heavy-ion damage such as Kr pre-irradiation can be used before helium irradiation to help induce a uniform distribution of small helium bubbles.
A helium fluence of about 3 × 10^16 ions/cm2 produces larger and denser bubbles and a higher hardness increment in Hf1Ta than a lower fluence.
Reactor-relevant irradiation temperatures can be selected that avoid phase transformations and significant segregation.
The expected helium bubbles have average sizes of approximately 10–14 nm.
Dislocation pinning by helium bubbles increases resistance to plastic deformation.
Severe lattice distortion in HEAs restricts defect-cluster formation and growth.
The inherent lattice distortion of the HEA limits helium-bubble overgrowth.
Limiting helium-bubble overgrowth maintains overall thermal and irradiation stability.
Relative to an unirradiated baseline, irradiated samples will have greater hardness and yield strength without significant phase-composition changes or elemental segregation.
The beneficial effect occurs only when irradiation parameters promote small-bubble formation.
Bubble overgrowth, coalescence, or blistering caused by excessive irradiation compromises mechanical performance and stability.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis specifies sub-10 nm helium bubbles, whereas the structural mediator specifies an average bubble size of approximately 10–14 nm.
